 When University of Wisconsin Law School graduate Scott Colom was interviewed by the school’s alumni magazine 11 years after he earned his degree in 2009, he was a highly regarded district attorney serving eastern Mississippi. He spoke about his innovative approaches to criminal justice and the courts. But, Colom added, “What I’ve got to do is get out of the courtroom more and be more of an advocate for what I’m trying to accomplish.”
 This year, Colom got out onto the federal campaign trail — with spectacular success.
 On Wednesday, he became the most unexpected winner of a U.S. Senate seat in an election cycle that produced more than its share of unexpected senators. Headlines around the world announced: “Mississippi elects Democrat Scott Colom as state’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction” and “Brutal Shock To Trump; Mississippi Gets First Black Senator Since 1874.”
 Colom began his 2026 Senate bid low on the pundit-compiled lists of Democrats who might finish as winners.
 Colom was running in a state that had backed Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential bid by a 61-38 margin. Not since 1982 had a Democrat won a U.S. Senate contest in Mississippi — and that Democrat was John Stennis, an arch segregationist who had held the seat since 1947.
 Stennis’s racism was such that he opposed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the national holiday honoring the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. One of Stennis’s predecessors, Jefferson Davis, served as president of the Confederacy during the Civil War.
 Only in the aftermath of that war, during the brief Reconstruction Era from 1865 to 1877, when the federal government intervened to defend the political rights of formerly enslaved people in the South, did Mississippi elect Black senators: Hiram Rhodes Revels and Blanche Kelso Bruce. Both served as Republicans. But they were Lincoln Republicans, from a time long before the modern era when the Grand Old Party moved far to the right and came to dominate the politics of Mississippi and other southern states.
 Colom thought he could break the pattern and move Mississippi in a new direction. His confidence was well-placed. By October of this year, when I visited him in his hometown of Columbus, Mississippi, his campaign was surging.
 Colom’s campaign slogan was “Mississippi Matters,” and he made the case that the state had suffered because so many of its political leaders had refused to embrace ideas that might allow it to progress economically and socially.
 “We’ve never been a lost cause; we’ve been a betrayed cause,” he told me.
 That argument made sense to the multiracial, multiethnic coalition of voters that, just a few weeks later, would propel him to victory over Trump-backed Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. As a seventh-generation Mississippian with a deep love of his state and a robust faith in its potential, Colom gave more credit to the voters than to himself.
 “Some folks are going to look at me, and they are going to say, ‘Wow, look at what Scott did,’” he said, when we discussed his campaign’s burgeoning momentum. “I didn't do this. The people of Mississippi did it.”
 How so?
 “They tested me. Listen, my first town hall, four people showed up. But I kept going … to town halls. I kept going to music festivals, I kept going to the housing projects,” explained Colom. “And the people said, ‘Listen, because he's the fighter for us, we going to fight for him.’”
 The crowds at the town hall gatherings grew to dozens, and then hundreds. And, when it came time to vote, nearly 500,000 Mississippians put trust in Scott Colom and the promise that “Mississippi Matters!”
 John Nichols is associate editor of The Capital Times.  jnichols@captimes.com  and @NicholsUprising.
